newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS SPOTLIGHT-HINGIS SQUEEZES OUT OF TIGHT CORNER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS SPOTLIGHT-HINGIS SQUEEZES OUT OF TIGHT CORNER.

text.p: World number one Martina Hingis flirted with French Open disaster on Thursday before accelerating clear of trouble against Italian second round opponent Gloria Pizzichini.

The top seed eventually won 3-6 6-4 6-1 to set up a teenage third round showdown with 15-year-old Anna Kournikova but will be increasingly vulnerable unless she can tighten up several areas of her game in the next few days.
No-one has beaten Hingis this year but Pizzichini, ranked 75th in the world, stood on the brink of doing so as she prepared to serve requiring a point for a 5-3 lead in the second set.
Had nerves not intervened and caused a double fault, the tournament would surely have lost the current darling of the women's game.
Instead, she was to win only one more game in the match and acknowledged later she had blown a major opportunity.

"It was a good chance for me but the minute I started thinking about it the match was finished, at my end at least. I was too afraid to win the match," said Pizzichini, a 21-year-old who reached the third round last year as a lucky loser.

"She wasn't playing very well, for sure. Last time I played her I lost 6-1 6-0 but this time her confidence wasn't great. I don't think she had a physical problem but perhaps she is not in the best condition."
Hingis certainly looked a little rusty after seven weeks out following her horse-riding accident last month and confessed she might have taken the hard-hitting, eager Italian too lightly.
"I played like...I want to say a bad word," grimaced Hingis. "I just couldn't hit the ball in the first set, I couldn't find my timing. I just hope it's better next time.
"When she was up 4-3 in the second and she made a double fault, I thought 'Thank God'. It wouldn't have been too good had I gone down 5-3.
"But I haven't played for seven weeks and I haven't got the eye for the shots that I usually have. My anticipation is not as good as it was when I won all the other tournaments."
Hingis is also discovering that some critics are not prepared to give her an easy ride when she turns in a poor performance.
One ungallant member of the media, determined to pry into areas which teenage girls normally discuss only with their best friends, asked her whether she was carrying any extra kilos.
"I don't think I have any," responded Hingis evenly. "This dress is pretty tight so I wouldn't be very happy with myself if I looked like a pig on court."
